title: Debugging a Process You Can't Read the Source Of: strace and the Syscall Boundary
objective: Use strace to observe what a running process is actually doing at the syscall boundary, independent of its source language, and recognize what that view can and can't reveal.

content_blocks.heading: Every Process Talks to the Kernel Through the Same Narrow Door
content_blocks.body:
A misbehaving service doesn't always come with readable source handy, time to dig through it, or even a known language -- but every process on Linux, regardless of what it's written in, interacts with the outside world through the same mechanism: system calls, the narrow interface a program crosses every time it opens a file, reads a socket, or spawns another process. Julia Evans's strace zine builds an entire debugging approach around exactly this: treat any program as a black box and watch its syscalls, the same way you'd sniff network traffic to debug a protocol you didn't write and have no source for.

This session covers that approach specifically: what `strace` actually shows, a worked example of using it to skip straight past a vague error message to the real cause, and -- just as importantly -- what it structurally can't tell you.

The mindset underneath all of it: a program's behavior is observable from the outside, through this one shared interface, even when nothing else about it is.

content_blocks.heading: A Syscall Is the One Boundary Every Program Has to Cross
content_blocks.body:
Opening a file, reading or writing data, making a network connection, forking a child process -- every one of these requires asking the kernel to do it, through a system call, because a regular program has no direct access to hardware or other processes on its own. `strace` attaches to a running process and prints every syscall it makes, with its arguments and return value, as it happens -- a complete, language-agnostic log of everything that process actually asked the kernel to do.

That language-agnosticism is the whole point: `strace` doesn't care whether the traced process is written in Python, Go, C, or something with no available source at all -- it's reading the one interface every one of them has to use identically, which is exactly what makes it useful on a process you can't otherwise inspect.

No instrumentation, logging statement, or debug build has to be added to the target process for any of this to work -- the trace happens entirely from the outside.

exercises.prompt: A team needs to debug a process, but doesn't have its source code and doesn't know what language it's written in. Why does `strace` still work here, when a source-level debugger couldn't?

options: strace observes syscalls, the one interface every process uses identically regardless of its source language or availability
strace actually decompiles the running process's machine code back into readable source, in whatever language it was written
strace only works on processes written in C, so this scenario would actually require installing a source-level debugger instead
strace requires the process's original source code to be present on disk somewhere, even if nobody currently has a copy of it
definition.explanation: strace doesn't need source code or even to know the implementation language -- it watches the syscall boundary, which every process has to cross for things like file access, network I/O, or spawning other processes, no matter what produced the binary. That's exactly why it works as a debugging tool when there's no source available at all.

content_blocks.heading: A Worked Example: "My Backup Script Keeps Failing"
content_blocks.body:
A backup script failing with a generic "permission denied" error leaves open exactly which file it was trying to access when it failed -- reading the whole script line by line to guess is slow, and the real answer might be a path that's only wrong in one specific environment. Running the script under `strace` and watching for the `open()` call that returns an error shows the exact path and exact error, immediately, without reading a line of the script's own logic.

This is the direct payoff of watching the syscall boundary instead of the program's own internal logic: the failure is visible exactly where it happens, as a specific syscall with a specific return value, rather than inferred from whatever the program's own error message happened to report (or failed to report with enough detail).

The same technique generalizes well beyond backups -- any "it just fails, I don't know why" report is a candidate for exactly this approach.

exercises.prompt: A backup script fails with a generic "permission denied" message, with no indication of which file caused it. Running it under `strace` shows an `open("/mnt/backup/db.sql", ...)` call returning `EACCES`. What did strace actually provide here?

options: The exact file path and syscall where the failure occurred, found without reading or guessing from the script's own source
A fix for the permission issue itself -- strace automatically repairs the problem it detects once it identifies the failing call
Proof that the script's own logic contains a bug, which is the only possible explanation for any syscall returning an error
Nothing beyond what the original error message already said; strace's output here is redundant with the script's own message
definition.explanation: The script's own "permission denied" message gave no file path; strace's syscall-level log showed exactly which `open()` call failed and on which path, immediately. strace only observes and reports -- it doesn't fix anything -- but that observation alone replaced what would otherwise be a guess-and-check read through the script's own logic.

content_blocks.heading: What strace Can't See: The Gaps Between Syscalls
content_blocks.body:
strace shows every syscall a process makes, but says nothing about what happens *between* two syscalls -- a long stretch of pure in-memory computation, with no file access or network activity at all, shows up in strace's output as simply nothing happening for a while. A program that's slow because of an inefficient in-memory loop, not because it's waiting on I/O, will look syscall-quiet in exactly the stretch where the real cost is.

That gap is itself a useful signal, not a dead end: a long pause with no syscalls narrows the search toward CPU-bound, in-process work -- exactly where a CPU profiler and flame graph (from the earlier Performance Engineering sessions) pick up where strace's syscall-level view runs out, the same "narrow down which category, then look inside it" shape as the USE method.

Misreading a quiet trace as "nothing is happening" instead of "the cost is in-process" is the specific mistake worth avoiding here.

exercises.prompt: strace shows a process making no syscalls at all for several seconds, right where it's known to be slow. What does this absence of syscalls most likely indicate?

options: The slowness is probably CPU-bound, in-process work -- exactly the gap a CPU profiler would need to look inside next
strace itself must be broken or misconfigured, since a genuinely slow process should always be making syscalls somewhere
The process silently crashed during that gap, even though it later resumes and keeps running completely normally afterward
This proves the slowness has nothing at all to do with performance, and must instead be a logic or correctness bug
definition.explanation: strace only has visibility into syscalls -- a gap with none happening means the process is doing something entirely in-process, like a computational loop, that never crosses the kernel boundary at all. That's not a strace failure; it's exactly the signal that points toward a CPU profiler as the next tool, the same way USE points from one resource to the specific tool suited to looking inside it.

content_blocks.heading: strace Has a Real Cost -- It's a Diagnostic Tool, Not a Default
content_blocks.body:
Tracing a process means the kernel pauses it at every single syscall to hand control to the tracer and back -- real overhead that scales with how syscall-heavy the traced program actually is. A process making thousands of small reads per second can slow down noticeably while being traced, which matters directly for whether it's safe to attach `strace` to something live in production versus a copy running in a safer, isolated environment first.

The practical rule: reach for `strace` as a targeted diagnostic for a specific question, on a process you've decided is safe to momentarily slow down -- not as something left attached by default, the same way a profiler or verbose logging isn't something you'd leave permanently enabled at full detail in a healthy system.

Filtering to specific syscall types, or tracing only briefly, are the usual ways to keep that overhead proportional to the question actually being asked.

exercises.prompt: A team wants to attach `strace` to a live, latency-sensitive production process making thousands of syscalls per second, just to "see what's going on" with no specific question in mind. What's the concern with this plan?

options: The per-syscall tracing overhead could noticeably slow this specific, syscall-heavy process while it's attached and running
There is no concern at all -- strace has zero measurable performance impact on any process, regardless of syscall volume
strace cannot attach to any process that is already running; it can only trace a process from the very moment it starts
This plan is fine specifically because the process is latency-sensitive -- strace's overhead only affects CPU-bound workloads
definition.explanation: Every syscall a traced process makes means pausing it and handing control to strace and back -- real overhead that compounds with how often the process actually makes syscalls. For a high-syscall-volume, latency-sensitive production process, attaching strace with no specific question to answer risks a real, user-visible slowdown for a fishing expedition rather than a targeted investigation.

content_blocks.heading: The Bottom Line
content_blocks.body:
Every process crosses the same syscall boundary to interact with the outside world, which is exactly what lets `strace` observe any process -- regardless of source availability or language -- by watching that one interface. A syscall-level trace can replace guessing at a vague error message with the exact failing call and its exact arguments, but it's blind to anything happening purely in-process between syscalls, which is itself a useful signal pointing toward a different tool (a CPU profiler) rather than a dead end. Tracing isn't free, either -- real per-syscall overhead makes it a targeted diagnostic, not something to leave running by default.

The common thread with this module's later sessions: a host-level problem is usually diagnosable by observing the right boundary directly, rather than guessing from symptoms alone.

The next sessions in this module move from this single-process view to the broader host: permissions and ownership, storage and mounts, and the networking and firewall layer a process's syscalls ultimately reach out through.
